title: A child at Patna
hook: Gobind Rai is born in Patna in 1666 and grows up playing at archery by the Ganges

segments.voice: Yesterday, carrying the head home: Bhai Jaita, Lakhi Shah, and the end of the ninth Guru's story. Your line was bring him home. Did you do a quiet kindness no one saw? Day eighty-one.

Everyone has a picture of themselves as a small child that the family loves to tell. The time you tried to feed the dog your broccoli. The summer you only answered to the name of a superhero. Those stories are small, but they're how a family says: we knew you before you were anyone. Today begins the last and longest part of this camp: the story of the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. Warrior, poet, founder of the Khalsa. But before any of that, there was a little boy in a city on the Ganges, far from Punjab, who had never met his father. Today, the child at Patna.
screen: `THE STORIES FAMILIES TELL.` → `THE TENTH GURU BEGINS.` → `A BOY ON THE GANGES.`

segments.voice: Remember day seventy-six: Guru Tegh Bahadur traveling east, leaving his wife, Mata Gujri, in Patna while he went on toward Assam. There, in Patna, in December 1666, their son was born. They named him Gobind Rai. His father was hundreds of miles away and would not see him for years. So the boy grew up in a household of women and Sikh families, his mother and his grandmother, Mata Nanaki, and his uncle Kirpal Chand, in a big city on a great river. Sikhs tell a handful of stories about those years, and they are full of play. The boy loved to lead the other children in mock battles, dividing them into two armies. He practiced archery by the river. Tradition says he would shoot small arrows, or toss things, at the women carrying water pots, cracking the pots, and his mother had to replace them. One story is especially tender. A local raja's wife, Rani Maini, had no children, and longed for a son. Tradition says the little boy came into her house and climbed into her lap, calling her mother, and she fed him boiled and salted chickpeas. At the gurdwara that stands there today, visitors are still given those chickpeas. In Patna the Sikh community remembers his birthplace with Takht Sri Patna Sahib, one of the five takhts. Hold onto this picture: a mischievous, warm, sporty boy, loved by a whole neighborhood. Around 1672 he was brought to Punjab, to his father at Anandpur. Everything else comes later.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a game you loved. Settle and breathe. Go back to being small. What did you play? Tag in the street. Pretend kitchens. A ball against a wall. Building forts out of couch cushions. Let one game come back in detail: the place, the other kids, the rules you made up, how it felt to be completely absorbed. Let yourself smile if you want to. That child is still in you. The bell holds the time.

howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Gobind Singh's birth each year with prayers and processions, and many visit Takht Sri Patna Sahib, the birthplace, and the gurdwara of Rani Maini, where boiled chickpeas are given as prasad.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Guru Gobind Singh's birth (December 1666) and childhood at Patna

notes: Birth date: traditionally 22 December 1666 (Poh sudi 7); the script says December 1666. Confirm.
Household: Mata Gujri, Mata Nanaki and Mata Gujri's brother Kirpal Chand; confirm.
The water-pot and Rani Maini (wife of Raja Fateh Chand Maini) stories are tradition; the gurdwara is Bal Lila Maini Sangat, where ghughnian (boiled chickpeas) are given. Confirm.
